title: Earthworm, Lumbricus Terrestris: A Novel Microinjection Vasculature In vivo Invertebrate Model
protocol: Turn on the micropipette puller and select a program to enter specific parameters for earthworm microinjection.
Set parameters to Pressure=500, Pull=75, Time=250, Heat=336, and Velocity=70.
Conduct a RAMP test to determine the heat value for the micropipettes before pulling them.
If the air pressure needs to be changed, press the clear button, select no (0) when asked to clear all values, and select change pressure (2).
Open the micropipette puller lid and load a micropipette into the puller.
Slide the pipette into the V-groove from the right along the pipette slit until the end of the pipette aligns with the end of the pipette holder.
Push the pipette as far as possible while ensuring that it remains resting on the pipette slit.
Lock in the pipette on the right side by tightening the knob.
Slide the locked system along with the pipette until it reaches the other side of the puller through the filament.
Lock in the left side of the pipette to the puller.
Close the puller and press the pull button.
Wait until the pipette is pulled before removing the two resulting pipettes.
Untighten the knobs to remove the pipettes carefully.
Place the pulled micropipettes on a micropipette holder or similar support for easy rotation without breaking the pipettes.
Capture a picture of the pulled micropipettes using a camera program at 10x magnification, approximately 1000 mm and 50 mm from the tip.
Ensure the camera settings match the microscope setting (10x) to measure accurately.
Select the camera on the camera software located on the top left corner.
Press the Snap button after focusing on the tip of the micropipette to get an accurate reading.
Take measurements of the pulled micropipettes to determine whether the desired tip size and consistency have been achieved.
Pull up to 5 pipettes to determine if the puller and its parameters are consistently producing the desired size.
Experiment with different settings until a desired tip size has been achieved if necessary.
Fix the filament and pipette placement according to the pipette puller manual if required.
Use a micropipette beveler with an electrode impedance meter and a 40x stereo microscope to bevel the pulled micropipettes.
Assemble the pedestal/grinding plate with the fine plate between the two black holders.
Place the bottom plate with magnets facing away from the plate.
Screw together the upper retaining ring, grinding fine plate, and lower retaining ring (magnetic).
Identify the purple abrasive surface of the grinding plate and ensure it faces upward.
Place five drops of beveler pedestal oil on the quartz optical flat.
Assemble the plate on top of the instrument with the oil.
Spin the plate manually to spread the oil evenly.
Turn on the instrument after manual spinning is complete.
Add saline onto the wick, which acts as a reference wire for the impedance meter.
Place the wick onto the beveling plate and soak the ribbon to create a circuit with the micropipette.
Cover the plate with a thin layer of saline solution.
Attach the lead segment to the end of the wire connected to the impedance meter.
Flip the "on" switch on the impedance meter and set it to standby mode.
Set the electrode impedance meter to x0.1 when ready to begin beveling.
Load the micropipette onto the pipette clamp located on the manipulator.
Tighten the knob of the pipette clamp to secure the micropipette during beveling.
Fill the entire micropipette with saline through its back end.
Insert the lead into the micropipette, ensuring there are no air bubbles.
Turn on the impedance meter by switching from "stand-by" to "x0.1".
Adjust the manipulator angle to 35° for consistent beveling of the tip.
Position the micropipette tip approximately two-thirds from the center of rotation of the grinding plate.
Lower the micropipette close to the plate using the coarse adjustment knob until it approaches the saline solution.
Look down the microscope to see the beveling process if no camera is available.
Verify that the impedance meter reading decreases to a value between 80 and 20 MΩ when the tip touches the saline.
Switch from coarse adjustment knob to fine adjustment knob for lowering pipette slowly.
Monitor impedance meter and tip simultaneously during beveling.
Observe changes in tip size and use lighting to improve visibility.
Lower the micropipette until it reaches the beveling plate.
Bevel the tip slowly until a resistance of approximately 20 M is reached.
Raise the micropipette from the beveler when resistance is achieved.
Remove the lead from the micropipette.
Unload the micropipette from the beveler.
Place the beveled micropipette on the micropipette holder.
Use the 10x objective on the microscope software to measure the tip opening size.
Confirm the microscope setting (10x) matches the camera settings before taking a picture.
Turn off the beveler by switching it to "off" on both the driving belt motor and the impedance meter.
Unscrew the pedestal/grinding plate to remove the upper retaining ring.
Slide the fine grinding plate off after lifting the upper retaining ring.
Remove the last magnetic attachment in order to clean all components.
Clean the pedestal, grinding plate, and quartz optical flat with deionized (DI) water and pat dry.
Remove excess oil on the quartz optical flat with laboratory wipes.
Wipe off the excess oil on the back of the grinding plate.
Use DI water on the beveler platform to remove any excess saline that may cause crystallization.
Squirt a small amount of DI water on the drive belt if the rotating magnetic base experiences jerking.
Wash beveled tips with DI water.
Lay clay inside a plate to hold micropipettes.
Make indentations in the clay for micropipette placement.
Cover the setup with a cover glass to prevent contamination.
Coat two plates with hydrophobic coating the day before use.
Shake the Base Coat can vigorously for one minute.
Spray the Base Coat onto the plate from 6-12 inches away, making light passes right to left and then up and down.
Shake the Top Coat can vigorously for one minute.
Spray the Top Coat onto the coated base from 6-12 inches away, making light passes right to left and then up and down.
Wait 1-2 minutes before applying an additional coating of the Base Coat.
Wait 30 minutes for the Base Coat to dry.
Repeat Steps 2.1.3 - 2.1.5 for the Top Coat.
Wait overnight or at least 12 hours for the plate to cure.
Fill the plate approximately halfway with mineral oil.
Place the plate with mineral oil onto the microinjector stage.
Load beveled tips on the microinjector.
Connect the microinjector directly to a laboratory compressed air jet.
Open the compressed air and set the low-pressure air-line regulator to 70 PSI.
Turn on the microinjector.
Backfill the tips with water using a 1 mL syringe with a Metal Hub Needle.
Load the micropipette onto the needle holder of the joystick micromanipulator.
Create water bubbles through the beveled micropipette for volume calibration.
Calibrate the microinjector to determine proper volume injection before compound administration into the earthworm vasculature.
Set the microinjector parameters at a pressure of 4 PSI and time of 0.5 seconds.
Position the pipette tip close to the bottom of the plate without breaking it.
Press the pedal to dispense a water bubble in the mineral oil.
If necessary, pull the plate away quickly from the bubble to separate it from the pipette tip.
Measure the bubble size using camera software or alternative software and calculate the volume.
Create 10 bubbles and measure their average diameter to determine the correct volume for dispensing into the earthworm vasculature.
Prepare 10% ethanol solution for earthworm anesthesia.
Place earthworms in a 100 mL beaker with soil between experiments.
Keep only 5 - 10 earthworms at a time in the beaker to prevent drying up.
Submerge earthworms in 10% ethanol for 30 minutes.
If earthworm movement persists after 30 minutes, leave it in ethanol for an additional 5 minutes.
Rinse the earthworm under faucet water to remove slime and ethanol.
Place the earthworm on a paper towel to remove excess water.
Once anesthetized, record each earthworm's weight (g), width (mm), length (mm), and vessel width (µm).
Take measurements before any incisions are made without stretching the earthworm.
Use a rubber pad during the surgical procedure to pin the earthworm down, exposing the vessel of interest.
Place the earthworm on its dorsal side with the darker part facing up.
Make a small side-incision on the skin of about 1 mm with a blade.
Create a long incision using surgical scissors from one pin location to another.
Pin the earthworm skin 33 mm apart, making a 27 mm opening to expose the vessel.
Use four pins initially and add or move pins as needed to properly expose the vessel.
Make an incision with surgical scissors to reach the other side of its body.
Push up toward the skin during the incision to prevent damage to internal structures.
Pin where the first incision was made and at the end of the cut for stability.
Use both surgical grips to move the skin, exposing the inside of the earthworm.
Pin down the skin on the bottom as the skin is moved over.
While moving up the earthworm, continue separating the skin from the organs carefully.
Once at the top, place the last pin.
If the vessel is not exposed, tug on opposite sides of the earthworm's skin to separate the elastic tissue.
Expose the ventral vessel by tugging on the skin if necessary.
Use the nerve cord as a marker for the ventral vessel.
If the ventral vessel is close to the gut, tug on the skin further to expose the vessel.
Push the gut to the side if needed but be cautious of creating a messy working area.
Face the dark part of the skin upward for exposing the dorsal vessel.
Use surgical scissors to cut toward the middle of the earthworm to the opposite side.
Make an incision from the middle of the earthworm toward the anterior portion, the head.
Push upward toward the skin during cutting to prevent damage to the inside of the earthworm.
Pin or re-pin the site of the first incision and then at the end of the cut that was made.
Place the earthworm on its ventral side.
Use four pins to hold down the skin of the earthworm and create a window to expose the vessel of interest.
Add an additional pin near the tip of the head, using a total of five pins.
Begin pinning from bottom to top, starting on the right side and moving to the left side.
Place two pins on the top near the tip of the head and two near the clitellum.
Make a small incision of about 1 mm on the side of the earthworm.
Use surgical scissors to cut toward the middle of the earthworm to the opposite side.
From the middle, make a cut toward the front of the earthworm until reaching the mouth.
Lift scissors against the skin to avoid cutting the vasculature when making an incision in the earthworm.
Make sure the cut is made to the anterior end of the earthworm for better visibility of the hearts.
Re-pin the earthworm if the skin curls into it during surgery.
Tug to separate tissue and properly expose the hearts.
Move white seminal vesicles around to locate the hearts hidden underneath them.
Move white seminal vesicles around to expose hearts if necessary.
Determine whether to move organs and tissue to locate the hearts of the earthworm.
Place the earthworm on the microinjection stage.
Use a lab wipe to remove any fluids around the vessel of interest, exposing the vasculature for injection.
Align the ventral vessel or perpendicular hearts to the micropipette.
Focus the microscope on the vasculature of interest.
Confirm joystick manipulators are set to 0 mm before lowering the micropipette.
Lower the micropipette tip in contact with the earthworm vessel.
Ensure the angle between the vessel and micropipette is less than 15°.
Begin applying pressure on the vessel with the micropipette.
Observe blood movement away from the tip due to vasculature pressure.
Use the joystick to move the micropipette forward for contact with the vasculature.
Move the tip along the direction of the dorsal and ventral vessels using coarse dial adjustments.
Penetrate the vessel slowly using fine control if necessary.
Press the pedal to inject the working solution into the vessel.
Observe blood dilution as an indicator of proper penetration.
Retract the micropipette slowly after injection.
Alternatively, break the tip while in the vessel to avoid blood loss.
